contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *shriveled*, *shriveling*. The British spelling *shrivelled* is common in books printed in the UK.

senses.gloss: Dried out and covered in wrinkles.
examples: I found two *shriveled* apples at the back of the drawer.
The flowers on the windowsill were brown and *shriveled*.
Without water the seedlings looked *more shriveled* every morning.

contrast: The verb's ordinary past participle is *shrunk* (*my sweater has shrunk*); *shrunken* is the adjective: *a shrunken sweater*.

senses.gloss: Smaller than it used to be, often in a way that looks wrong.
examples: He pulled a *shrunken* wool sweater out of the dryer.
Her grandfather seemed *shrunken* after the illness.
The company is trying to run on a *shrunken* budget.

position: predicative only — *the door is shut*; before a noun use *closed*
contrast: Don't say *a shut door* — before a noun Americans say *a closed door*. The verb is the same in all three forms: *shut*, *shut*, *shut*.

senses.gloss: Closed, not open.
examples: Make sure the windows are *shut* before you leave.
Her eyes were tightly *shut*.
The lid won't stay *shut*.

senses.gloss: Not open for business.
examples: The pharmacy is *shut* on Sundays.
By ten the whole town is *shut*.

senses.gloss: Closed down, out of business for good.
examples: The main street is lined with *shuttered* stores.
They bought a *shuttered* factory and turned it into lofts.
The restaurant has been *shuttered* since March.

senses.gloss: With the shutters closed over the windows.
examples: The house sat dark and *shuttered* all winter.
We walked past rows of *shuttered* windows.

contrast: *Siam* is the old name of Thailand, so the modern word for the country is *Thai*. *Siamese* survives mainly in *Siamese cat*; for *Siamese twins* doctors now say *conjoined twins*.

senses.gloss: Of Siam, the old name of Thailand — now used mostly in fixed phrases.
examples: They have two *Siamese* cats with bright blue eyes.
The museum has a room of *Siamese* art.
My grandmother still calls conjoined twins *Siamese* twins.

comparison: not gradable — but *very Siberian* when it means 'bitterly cold'
contrast: The person is the noun *a Siberian*. Americans often use it loosely for extreme cold: *Siberian temperatures* in Chicago.

senses.gloss: Of or from Siberia.
examples: A *Siberian* husky needs a lot of exercise.
The cold front brought *Siberian* air all the way to Texas.
Her family is *Siberian*, from a village near Irkutsk.

contrast: The person is the noun *a Sicilian*. Sicily is part of Italy, so someone can be both *Italian* and *Sicilian*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Sicily.
examples: This is my great-aunt's *Sicilian* recipe for eggplant.
The pizza place does a thick *Sicilian* crust.
Both of his parents are *Sicilian*.

senses.gloss: So bad or cruel that it shocks and disgusts you.
examples: It was *sickening* to watch him blame the kids.
The details that came out in court were *sickening*.
There is something *sickening* about that much waste.

senses.gloss: Making you feel physically ill.
examples: A *sickening* smell of gas filled the hallway.
The car hit the guardrail with a *sickening* thud.

contrast: Despite the *-ly*, *sickly* is an adjective, not an adverb. It is not the same as *sick*: a *sick* child is ill today, a *sickly* child is ill again and again.

senses.gloss: Often ill and not strong.
examples: He was a *sickly* kid who missed half of third grade.
The kitten was the *sickliest* of the litter.
She looked pale and *sickly* after the flight.

senses.gloss: Unpleasant in a weak, too-sweet or washed-out way.
examples: The waiting room was painted a *sickly* green.
The punch had a *sickly* sweet taste.

form: compound — noun + *-ing* participle, from the idea of laughing until your sides hurt
contrast: Also written *side-splitting*. It is strong praise, so save it for something truly funny.

senses.gloss: Extremely funny.
examples: His impression of the principal was *sidesplitting*.
We watched a *sidesplitting* comedy about a family road trip.
The second act is *more sidesplitting* than the first.

contrast: *sideways* is much more often an adverb (*he stepped sideways*, *turn it sideways*). As an adjective it goes only before a noun.

senses.gloss: Pointing or facing toward the side.
examples: She gave him a *sideways* look and said nothing.
The crab made a quick *sideways* move.
He answered with a *sideways* nod toward the door.

contrast: Two words, both capitalized, and the person is the noun *a Sierra Leonean*. The country is *Sierra Leone*, with no *-an*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Sierra Leone.
examples: The *Sierra Leonean* team qualified for the first time.
She writes about *Sierra Leonean* music for a magazine.
Our new neighbors are *Sierra Leonean*.

contrast: The *g* is silent: SYND, one syllable.

senses.gloss: With a signature on it.
examples: Bring a *signed* copy of the lease to the office.
The contract isn't *signed* yet.
He keeps a *signed* baseball on his desk.

contrast: In research *statistically significant* means only that the result is unlikely to be chance — not that it is large.

senses.gloss: Large or important enough to matter.
examples: There has been a *significant* drop in traffic deaths.
The repair will cost a *significant* amount of money.
This is the *most significant* change to the law in thirty years.

senses.gloss: Carrying a meaning that is not said out loud.
examples: She gave her husband a *significant* look across the table.
It is *significant* that he never mentioned the money.

contrast: Pronounced SEEK, like the verb *seek*. It is also the noun for a member of the religion (*a Sikh*); the religion itself is *Sikhism*.

senses.gloss: Of the Sikh religion, which began in the Punjab, or of its followers.
examples: There is a *Sikh* temple on the edge of town.
Many *Sikh* men wear a turban.
His family is *Sikh*.

takes: *about* or *on* + noun, in the 'saying nothing' sense

senses.gloss: Making no sound at all.
examples: The house was *silent* except for the clock.
The new dishwasher is almost completely *silent*.
We stood in a *silent* line outside the door.

senses.gloss: Saying nothing, especially about something people expect you to speak about.
examples: The company has been *silent* about the layoffs.
He stayed *silent* for the whole meeting.

senses.gloss: Not pronounced, or made without recorded sound.
examples: The *b* in 'climb' is *silent*.
She wrote her thesis on *silent* films.

senses.gloss: Soft and smooth to the touch, like silk.
examples: The puppy has *silky* black ears.
This shampoo leaves your hair *silkier*.
She ran her hand over the *silky* fabric.

senses.gloss: Smooth and pleasant in sound or taste.
examples: He has a *silky* radio voice.
The sauce was rich and *silky*.

position: attributive only — mostly before a noun
contrast: It is half a compliment: a *silver-tongued* speaker is smooth, and often a little too smooth to trust.

senses.gloss: Able to talk people into things with charming, persuasive speech.
examples: A *silver-tongued* lawyer got the whole case thrown out.
He was the *silver-tongued* one; his brother just nodded.
Even the *most silver-tongued* salesman couldn't move that car.

senses.gloss: Shining pale gray, like silver.
examples: The lake looked *silvery* under the moon.
He has a full head of *silvery* hair.
The fish flashed *silvery* in the net.

senses.gloss: Clear and light in sound.
examples: Her *silvery* laugh carried across the yard.
Somewhere below, a *silvery* bell rang twice.

contrast: Used about a person it is an insult, and about someone with a disability it is offensive; say *has a learning disability* instead.

senses.gloss: Too simple to deal with something complicated.
examples: That is a *simple-minded* answer to a hard question.
Their plan is *simple-minded*: build more parking and hope.

senses.gloss: Not clever, and easy to fool.
examples: The movie treats its audience as *simple-minded*.
He plays a sweet, *simple-minded* farmhand.

senses.gloss: Made easier to understand or to use, with the hard parts taken out.
examples: The bank sent out a *simplified* version of the contract.
We read a *simplified* edition of the novel in class.
The new form is much *more simplified* than the old one.

contrast: Not a fancy word for *simple*. *Simple* is usually good (*a simple plan*); *simplistic* is always a criticism — it means too simple to be true.

senses.gloss: Treating something complicated as if it were easy, and so getting it wrong.
examples: That's a *simplistic* view of what caused the war.
His answer was *simplistic*, and the reporters said so.
Blaming one department is the *most simplistic* explanation there is.

position: attributive only — mostly before a noun

senses.gloss: Made by a computer or a machine to copy real conditions.
examples: Pilots train in a *simulated* landing before they ever fly.
The lab ran a *simulated* power outage.
Students take a *simulated* exam in the first week.

senses.gloss: Made to look like a more expensive material.
examples: The seats are *simulated* leather.
She wore a ring with a *simulated* diamond.

position: attributive only — mostly before a noun; after a verb use *at the same time*
contrast: Americans say sy-muhl-TAY-nee-uhs; the British start it sim-. The adverb is *simultaneously*, and it is what you usually need after a verb.

senses.gloss: Happening at exactly the same time as something else.
examples: The band played *simultaneous* shows in three cities by video.
The conference offers *simultaneous* translation into four languages.
The launch was *simultaneous* with the announcement in Tokyo.

contrast: The fixed phrases keep an old superlative: *my sincerest apologies*, *sincerest thanks*. Letters end *Sincerely*, not *Sincere*.

senses.gloss: Really meaning what you say, with nothing put on.
examples: Her apology sounded *sincere*.
He is *sincere* about wanting to help.
Of all the speeches that night, hers was the *most sincere*.

senses.gloss: Morally wrong, especially in a religious sense.
examples: The sermon called gossip *sinful*.
He grew up in a house where dancing was *sinful*.
They treat waste as *more sinful* than anything else.

senses.gloss: So rich or enjoyable that it feels like cheating — used as a joke.
examples: That chocolate cake is downright *sinful*.
A nap at two in the afternoon feels *sinful*.

contrast: The person is the noun *a Singaporean*. The country is *Singapore*, with no *-an*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Singapore.
examples: We had *Singaporean* noodles at a stand downtown.
The fund is run by a *Singaporean* bank.
Her husband is *Singaporean*.

position: attributive only — *a single mistake*; but *she is single* in the 'not married' sense
contrast: *a single ticket* in the US means one ticket; the British one-way ticket is a *one-way* in American English.

senses.gloss: Only one, and no more — often for emphasis.
examples: Not a *single* person showed up.
He answered every *single* question.
One *single* mistake cost them the game.

senses.gloss: Not married and not in a relationship.
examples: She's been *single* since the divorce.
It's a hard schedule for a *single* parent.

senses.gloss: Meant for one person.
examples: The room has two *single* beds.
I booked a *single* room for Thursday night.

senses.gloss: Of a jacket or coat: closing with one row of buttons.
examples: He wore a plain *single-breasted* navy suit.
The jacket is *single-breasted*, with two buttons.
A *single-breasted* coat is easier to wear open.

position: attributive only — mostly before a noun
contrast: The scientific word is *unicellular*; *single-celled* is what a textbook or a teacher says.

senses.gloss: Made of only one cell.
examples: Bacteria are *single-celled* organisms.
Life on Earth was *single-celled* for billions of years.
We looked at a *single-celled* alga under the microscope.

contrast: After a verb use the adverb: *she did it single-handedly*, not *she did it single-handed*.

senses.gloss: Done by one person with no help.
examples: His *single-handed* rescue of the crew made the news.
It was a *single-handed* sail across the Atlantic.
The report credits her with a *single-handed* turnaround.

senses.gloss: Giving all your attention to one goal and nothing else.
examples: She is *single-minded* about getting into medical school.
It took *single-minded* work to finish the bridge on time.
He is the *most single-minded* person on the team.

senses.gloss: Typed with no blank line between the lines of text.
examples: He handed in four *single-spaced* pages.
The résumé should be *single-spaced*.
A *single-spaced* letter is hard to mark up.

contrast: The grammar sense is the everyday one. The 'remarkable' sense is formal and goes before a noun: *a singular talent*.

senses.gloss: In grammar: naming one, not more than one.
examples: 'Child' is *singular* and 'children' is plural.
The verb has to agree with a *singular* subject.
*Singular* 'they' is now standard in American writing.

senses.gloss: Unusual and remarkable — formal.
examples: She has a *singular* gift for calming a room.
The building is a *singular* piece of American design.

senses.gloss: Giving the feeling that something evil or harmful is going on.
examples: There was something *sinister* about the empty parking garage.
He plays a quiet, *sinister* landlord.
The second letter was *more sinister* than the first.

contrast: Despite the *-ly*, this is an adjective, not an adverb. The male pair is *brotherly*.

senses.gloss: Of or like a sister — warm, protective and close.
examples: She gave him a *sisterly* pat on the shoulder.
There is a *sisterly* feeling between the two teams.
That was the *most sisterly* thing anyone did for me all year.

position: attributive only — mostly before a noun
form: from *Sisyphus*, the Greek king made to roll a rock uphill forever
contrast: Capitalized, because it comes from a name. Russian has the same image: *сизифов труд*.

senses.gloss: Endless and hopeless, because the work undoes itself.
examples: Keeping the kitchen clean with three kids is a *Sisyphean* task.
Answering that inbox is *Sisyphean* labor.
He described the cleanup as a *Sisyphean* effort with no end date.

contrast: *The president is sitting* is the verb, not this adjective. Note the idiom *a sitting duck* — an easy target. *Sitting room* for *living room* is chiefly British.

senses.gloss: Holding the office right now.
examples: No *sitting* senator has lost that seat in forty years.
The *sitting* judge recused herself.
It is rare for a *sitting* mayor to be challenged in the primary.

senses.gloss: Done in a seated position.
examples: Measure the chair from the floor in a *sitting* position.
The stretch can be done from a *sitting* pose.

position: after the noun — *a house situated on the lake*; also after *be*
contrast: Don't put it before a noun — not *a situated house*. In everyday speech *located* or plain *is* sounds less formal: *The hotel is on the beach*.

senses.gloss: Standing in a particular place — formal, common in ads and reports.
examples: The cabin is *situated* on twelve acres of woods.
We stayed at a hotel *situated* right on the beach.
The plant is *situated* between two rivers.

senses.gloss: In a particular position, especially about money — with *well* or *badly*.
examples: After the sale they were comfortably *situated*.
Small farms are badly *situated* to survive a dry year.

contrast: *sixty* counts, *sixtieth* puts in order: *sixty years* but *the sixtieth year*. It is also the noun for the fraction 1/60: *a sixtieth of a second*.

senses.gloss: Coming after fifty-nine others in a series.
examples: We threw a party for my mother's *sixtieth* birthday.
This is the museum's *sixtieth* year.
She was the *sixtieth* caller and won the tickets.

position: attributive only — mostly before a noun
contrast: American writing drops the *e*: *sizable*. The spelling *sizeable* is usual in Britain.

senses.gloss: Fairly large.
examples: They left a *sizable* tip.
A *sizable* crowd waited outside the courthouse.
The grant covers a *sizable* part of the cost.

senses.gloss: Cooking with the hissing sound of hot fat.
examples: The waiter brought out a *sizzling* plate of fajitas.
Bacon was *sizzling* in the pan when I came downstairs.

senses.gloss: Extremely hot.
examples: We crossed the *sizzling* parking lot in flip-flops.
The forecast calls for another *sizzling* weekend.

senses.gloss: Exciting, full of energy or passion.
examples: The two leads have *sizzling* chemistry.
The band opened with a *sizzling* guitar solo.

senses.gloss: Of the bones of the body.
examples: The X-ray showed no *skeletal* damage.
The class covers the *skeletal* system.

senses.gloss: So thin that the bones show.
examples: The dog they rescued was *skeletal*.
He came back from the hospital looking *skeletal*.

senses.gloss: Cut back to the bare minimum.
examples: The office runs on a *skeletal* staff over the holidays.
All I have so far is a *skeletal* outline.

contrast: American spelling starts with *sk-*; the British write *sceptical*. It means doubting, not *pessimistic*.

senses.gloss: Doubting that something is true, honest or going to work.
examples: The neighbors were *skeptical* about the new parking plan.
He gave me a *skeptical* look.
Voters are *more skeptical* than they were a year ago.

contrast: The 'suspicious' sense is everyday American slang and is what you will hear most: *a sketchy guy*, *a sketchy neighborhood*.

senses.gloss: Not to be trusted; a little dangerous or dishonest — informal.
examples: That website looks *sketchy* — don't put your card in.
We walked home through a *sketchy* part of town.
The deal got *sketchier* the more he explained it.

senses.gloss: Giving only a rough idea, without the details.
examples: Details of the crash are still *sketchy*.
My memory of that summer is pretty *sketchy*.

takes: *toward* or *in favor of* + noun; *by* + noun for the cause

senses.gloss: Twisted away from a fair or true picture.
examples: The results were *skewed* by two huge donations.
The sample is *skewed* toward older voters.
Their coverage is *more skewed* than they admit.

senses.gloss: Sitting at a crooked angle.
examples: The picture over the couch was *skewed*.
One *skewed* shelf threw off the whole wall.

contrast: American spelling has two *l*'s: *skillful*. The British write *skilful*.

senses.gloss: Doing something well, because of training and practice.
examples: She is a *skillful* negotiator.
He is *skillful* at getting kids to talk.
That was the *most skillful* piece of driving I've ever seen.

contrast: In the US it is *skim milk*; the British say *skimmed milk*. Don't confuse it with the verb *skim* — to read something quickly.

senses.gloss: Of milk: with the cream taken off.
examples: I take my coffee with *skim* milk.
The recipe calls for a cup of *skim* milk.
Does this latte have *skim* milk in it?

senses.gloss: Of clothes: very small, covering very little.
examples: She said the costume was too *skimpy* for a school play.
He showed up in *skimpy* running shorts.

senses.gloss: Not as much as you need or expect.
examples: The portions were *skimpy* for the price.
This year's benefits package is *skimpier* than last year's.

position: predicative only — mostly after a verb
contrast: It comes from the saying *Beauty is only skin-deep*, and it is still used mostly in that shape: *only skin-deep*.

senses.gloss: Only on the surface, not real or lasting.
examples: Beauty is only *skin-deep*.
His politeness is *skin-deep* — watch how he treats waiters.
The changes at the company turned out to be *skin-deep*.

contrast: Usually written as one word in American English: *skintight*. Both spellings are correct.

senses.gloss: Fitting as closely as skin.
examples: The cyclists wore *skin-tight* suits.
Her dress was black and *skin-tight*.
He can't stand *skin-tight* sleeves.

contrast: *skinny* is blunt and can sting; *slim* and *slender* are compliments, *thin* is neutral.

senses.gloss: Very thin, often too thin.
examples: He was a *skinny* kid with big glasses.
The cat got *skinnier* every week until we took her to the vet.

senses.gloss: Of clothes: cut very narrow.
examples: He wears *skinny* jeans and high-tops.
A *skinny* tie looks odd with that suit.

senses.gloss: Of a coffee drink: made with nonfat milk — informal.
examples: She ordered a *skinny* vanilla latte.
Can you make that one *skinny*?

contrast: The same word as *skin-tight*; American writing usually closes it up.

senses.gloss: Fitting as closely as skin.
examples: The dancers wore *skintight* black leggings.
That shirt is *skintight* on him now.
She bought a *skintight* swimsuit for the meet.

senses.gloss: Of an animal: nervous and easily frightened.
examples: The horse is *skittish* around loud trucks.
Our rescue dog was *skittish* for the first month.

senses.gloss: Of people or markets: nervous and quick to back out.
examples: Investors are *skittish* about the new tariffs.
Buyers got *more skittish* as the rates went up.

senses.gloss: Of the light blue of a clear sky.
examples: She painted the nursery *sky-blue*.
He wore a *sky-blue* shirt with no tie.
The team's away jerseys are *sky-blue*.

contrast: The noun is in *cut me some slack* (go easy on me), and *slacks* means dress pants.

senses.gloss: Loose, not pulled tight.
examples: The rope went *slack* and the boat drifted.
Keep the line a little *slacker* or it will snap.

senses.gloss: With little business or activity.
examples: January is the *slack* season at the store.
Demand has been *slack* since the spring.

senses.gloss: Not careful enough about doing a job properly.
examples: Security at the gate has gotten *slack*.
He was fired for *slack* record-keeping.

contrast: Everyday English says *killed*; *slain* survives in news writing, in the Bible and in fantasy. After a verb say *was killed*, not *was slain*.

senses.gloss: Killed, especially violently — formal and journalistic.
examples: The city named a park after the *slain* officer.
Families of the *slain* students spoke at the hearing.
The report lists the names of the *slain* soldiers.

contrast: In American law *slander* is spoken and *libel* is written, so a magazine article is *libelous*, not *slanderous*.

senses.gloss: Saying untrue things that damage someone's good name.
examples: He called the accusation *slanderous* and hired a lawyer.
The radio host made *slanderous* remarks about the sheriff.
Her second statement was *more slanderous* than the first.

senses.gloss: Sloping, not straight up and down or flat.
examples: The attic has a *slanted* ceiling.
Her handwriting is small and *slanted*.

senses.gloss: Presented in an unfair way that favors one side.
examples: The coverage was badly *slanted* toward the developer.
Both sides say the questions were *slanted*.

form: compound — *slap* + *dash*, the sound of working too fast

senses.gloss: Done in a hurry and without care.
examples: The paint job was *slapdash* — you can see the tape lines.
He turned in a *slapdash* report an hour before the deadline.
This repair is even *more slapdash* than the last one.

senses.gloss: Cut with long, violent cuts.
examples: He came out to four *slashed* tires.
The painting was found *slashed* in the basement.

senses.gloss: Cut sharply, about prices or budgets.
examples: The store advertised *slashed* prices on winter coats.
Libraries are working with *slashed* budgets.

position: attributive only — mostly before a noun
contrast: A word from American history, used about the South before the Civil War. The noun for the person is *a slaveholder*; writers today often prefer *enslaver*.

senses.gloss: Owning enslaved people, or allowing people to be owned.
examples: Most of the early presidents came from *slaveholding* families.
The compromise kept the number of *slaveholding* states even.
The museum sits on a former *slaveholding* plantation.

contrast: *Slavic* covers a language family and the peoples who speak it, so a Russian, a Pole and a Serb are all *Slavic*. Don't confuse it with *slavish*, which means copying without thought.

senses.gloss: Of the Slavic peoples or their languages.
examples: Russian and Polish are both *Slavic* languages.
She teaches *Slavic* literature at a state university.
The neighborhood is old and heavily *Slavic*.

position: attributive only — mostly before a noun
contrast: Not the same as *Slavic* (of the Slavs), and the two are pronounced differently: SLAY-vish and SLAH-vik.

senses.gloss: Copying something exactly, with no ideas of your own.
examples: The building is a *slavish* copy of a Paris train station.
His writing is a *slavish* imitation of Hemingway.

senses.gloss: Obeying or admiring someone far too much.
examples: The party demands *slavish* loyalty.
She warned against *slavish* devotion to the rankings.

senses.gloss: Dishonest and morally dirty.
examples: It was a *sleazy* move to read her texts.
He got rich running a *sleazy* loan business.

senses.gloss: Cheap, dirty and a little dangerous.
examples: They stayed at a *sleazy* motel off the highway.
The bar got *sleazier* after the new owners took over.

senses.gloss: Smooth, shiny and healthy-looking.
examples: The horse had a *sleek* brown coat.
She pulled her hair back into a *sleek* ponytail.

senses.gloss: Elegant, with clean lines and no clutter.
examples: They drove up in a *sleek* black sedan.
The new phone is even *sleeker* than the last one.

contrast: After a verb, *the baby is sleeping* is the verb; the adjective there is *asleep*: *the baby is asleep*. In *sleeping bag* and *sleeping pill* the word says what it is for, not that it sleeps.

senses.gloss: Asleep right now.
examples: Don't wake the *sleeping* baby.
He stepped over two *sleeping* dogs to get to the door.
Careful — there are *sleeping* kids in the next room.

senses.gloss: Spent without sleep, or unable to sleep.
examples: I spent a *sleepless* night waiting for the call.
Three *sleepless* weeks with a newborn left them both foggy.
She lay *sleepless* until the sky turned gray.

senses.gloss: Wanting to go to sleep.
examples: The medicine makes me *sleepy*.
He gets *sleepier* right after lunch.

senses.gloss: Quiet, with very little going on.
examples: They retired to a *sleepy* town on the coast.
It was a *sleepy* Sunday afternoon.

senses.gloss: Made with no sleeves.
examples: She wore a *sleeveless* summer dress.
The dress code says no *sleeveless* shirts.
His jersey is *sleeveless*.

comparison: -er/-est or more/most — *slenderer*, *slenderest*; more often *more slender*, *most slender*
contrast: *slender* is a compliment, like *slim*; *skinny* is blunt and *thin* is neutral.

senses.gloss: Thin in a graceful, attractive way.
examples: She has long, *slender* fingers.
The dancer was tall and *slender*.
The second vase is *more slender* than the first.

senses.gloss: Small in amount, and barely enough.
examples: The bill passed by a *slender* majority.
They are living on a *slender* income.

contrast: It is in the American joke *the best thing since sliced bread* — the greatest invention there is.

senses.gloss: Cut into thin flat pieces.
examples: Buy a pound of *sliced* turkey at the deli.
Top it with *sliced* almonds.
The bread comes *sliced*.

senses.gloss: Smooth and slippery, usually because it is wet.
examples: The roads were *slick* with freezing rain.
The deck gets *slicker* than it looks after a shower.

senses.gloss: Done smoothly and well.
examples: That was a *slick* piece of editing.
The company put out a *slick* thirty-second ad.

senses.gloss: Smooth in a way that makes you suspicious.
examples: A *slick* salesman talked them into the extended warranty.
His answers were too *slick* to believe.

senses.gloss: That opens by sliding instead of swinging.
examples: The kitchen has a *sliding* glass door to the deck.
Push the *sliding* panel to the left.
The van has a *sliding* side door.

senses.gloss: Changing with the circumstances, about a rate or a scale.
examples: The clinic charges on a *sliding* scale based on income.
Daycare fees follow a *sliding* scale.

position: attributive only — *a slight delay*; the 'thin' sense also goes after a verb
contrast: The superlative lives in two fixed phrases: *not in the slightest* (not at all) and *the slightest idea*. There is also a noun and a verb *slight*, meaning an insult.

senses.gloss: Very small in degree.
examples: There's a *slight* delay on the eastbound train.
She has a *slight* accent.
I don't have the *slightest* idea where he went.

senses.gloss: Thin and delicate in build.
examples: He is a *slight* man with quick movements.
She looked too *slight* to carry the pack.

senses.gloss: Covered with something wet, thick and unpleasant.
examples: The rocks by the creek are *slimy*.
The lettuce at the bottom of the bag had gone *slimy*.

senses.gloss: Friendly in a false, unpleasant way.
examples: There's something *slimy* about that landlord.
He is the *slimiest* guy in the office.

contrast: *a slippery slope* means one small step that leads to something much worse.

senses.gloss: Hard to stand on or hold, because it is smooth or wet.
examples: The steps get *slippery* when it rains.
Wet leaves make the sidewalk *slipperier* than ice.

senses.gloss: Not to be trusted, and hard to pin down.
examples: He is a *slippery* witness who changes his story.
'Fair' is a *slippery* word in this contract.

senses.gloss: Done carelessly, without attention to the details.
examples: The inspector called the wiring *slipshod* and dangerous.
*Slipshod* record-keeping cost the clinic its license.
This draft is *more slipshod* than anything he's turned in before.

senses.gloss: Going up or down at an angle instead of lying flat.
examples: The house sits on a gently *sloping* lawn.
Watch your head under the *sloping* ceiling.
The field is *sloping*, so the water runs to the road.

senses.gloss: Done carelessly and full of mistakes.
examples: The report was full of *sloppy* math.
Their defense got *sloppier* in the fourth quarter.

senses.gloss: Messy or loose-looking.
examples: He came to dinner in a *sloppy* old sweatshirt.
Her handwriting is *sloppy* but readable.

form: -ed from *slosh*, the sound of liquid moving around
contrast: Slang, and slightly old-fashioned but still understood. It goes after a verb only — never *a sloshed man*.

senses.gloss: Drunk — informal.
examples: He got completely *sloshed* at the reception.
Half the wedding party was *sloshed* by nine.
You don't want to be *sloshed* when your boss shows up.

contrast: Formal and a little old-fashioned — everyday English says *lazy*. *Sloth* is also one of the seven deadly sins, and the name of the animal.

senses.gloss: Lazy, unwilling to work or move.
examples: He wrote about a *slothful* nephew who never left the couch.
Two weeks of vacation left me *slothful*.
The sermon called idleness the *most slothful* kind of sin.

contrast: *Slovak* is the shorter adjective and the name of the language and the people; *Slovakian* usually means 'of the country'. Slovakia is not Slovenia.

senses.gloss: Of or from Slovakia.
examples: He plays for a *Slovakian* hockey club.
We tried a *Slovakian* dumpling dish at the festival.
Her mother is *Slovakian*.

contrast: Slovenia borders Italy and Austria; Slovakia is farther east. The short form *Slovene* is also used for the language.

senses.gloss: Of or from Slovenia.
examples: The *Slovenian* Alps are full of small ski towns.
She translates *Slovenian* poetry.
Both coaches are *Slovenian*.

contrast: Despite the *-ly*, this is an adjective, not an adverb. It has nothing to do with *Slovenian*.

senses.gloss: Messy and careless about how you look or work.
examples: The sergeant called his uniform *slovenly*.
She has *slovenly* habits in the kitchen.
His desk is the *most slovenly* one on the floor.

contrast: The adverb is *slowly*: *drive slowly*. *Drive slow* and *go slow* are heard in speech and on signs, but write *slowly*.

senses.gloss: Not moving quickly.
examples: Traffic was *slow* the whole way home.
She's the *slowest* runner on the team, and she still finished.

senses.gloss: Taking a long time to happen or to get done.
examples: Recovery after the surgery was *slow*.
He was *slow* to answer my email.

senses.gloss: With little business or activity.
examples: Tuesday nights are *slow* at the restaurant.
It's been a *slow* month for sales.

senses.gloss: Of a clock or watch: showing a time earlier than the real one.
examples: The kitchen clock is five minutes *slow*.
My watch runs *slow* in the cold.

senses.gloss: Moving slowly.
examples: A *slow-moving* storm is sitting over the valley.
We were stuck behind a *slow-moving* tractor.

senses.gloss: Going forward or selling slowly.
examples: The store marked down its *slow-moving* inventory.
It is a *slow-moving* case that has been in court for years.

contrast: An insult — use it about a character in a book, not about a person you know.

senses.gloss: Slow to understand things.
examples: The play makes the sheriff look *slow-witted*.
I felt *slow-witted* after three hours of jet lag.
He writes the villain as cruel and the henchman as *slow-witted*.

senses.gloss: Moving or working more slowly than it should.
examples: The engine is *sluggish* on cold mornings.
I feel *sluggish* if I skip breakfast.

senses.gloss: With little growth or activity, about business.
examples: Home sales have been *sluggish* all spring.
The economy looks *more sluggish* than it did in January.

senses.gloss: Of speech: with the words running together and hard to make out.
examples: His speech was *slurred* and the nurse called the doctor.
She left a *slurred* message at two in the morning.
*Slurred* words can be a sign of a stroke.

senses.gloss: Covered with or made of half-melted snow.
examples: The sidewalks were gray and *slushy*.
Wear boots — the driveway is *slushy*.
The roads get *slushier* once the plows come through.

contrast: *small* is a plain measurement; *little* often adds feeling (*a little cabin* sounds fond). Use *small* after *how*: *How small is it?*

senses.gloss: Not big in size or amount.
examples: They live in a *small* apartment near the park.
Do you have this shirt in a *smaller* size?

senses.gloss: Young.
examples: She has two *small* children at home.
I remember that song from when I was *small*.

senses.gloss: Not important.
examples: It's a *small* problem — we can fix it today.
That is a *small* price to pay for a quiet street.

contrast: A finance word: it describes the size of the company, not the price of the share.

senses.gloss: Of a company whose total stock value is small.
examples: He put part of his savings in a *small-cap* fund.
*Small-cap* stocks swing more than the big names.
The index tracks about two thousand *small-cap* companies.

senses.gloss: Interested only in small things, and unwilling to accept other people's ideas.
examples: It was a *small-minded* rule about who could park where.
He left town to get away from *small-minded* gossip.
The longer the argument went on, the *more small-minded* both sides sounded.

senses.gloss: Done at a limited size, not across a whole country or industry.
examples: They started with a *small-scale* pilot in two schools.
*Small-scale* farmers can't compete on price.
For now the project is deliberately *small-scale*.

senses.gloss: Working on a small, unimportant level — usually said with a shrug.
examples: He was a *small-time* dealer who got caught in a big case.
They started as a *small-time* operation out of a garage.
She is tired of *small-time* clients and the fees that come with them.

contrast: The *-ish* softens the word: *smallish* means fairly small, and avoids sounding too definite.

senses.gloss: Fairly small.
examples: It's a *smallish* town, maybe nine thousand people.
He ordered a *smallish* coffee and sat by the window.
The yard is *smallish* but the house is bright.

senses.gloss: Polite and flattering in a way that feels false and unpleasant.
examples: The host has a *smarmy* way of complimenting people.
He sent a *smarmy* thank-you note to the whole board.
That ad is the *smarmiest* thing on television.

contrast: In American English the first meaning is *intelligent*; in Britain *smart* usually means well-dressed. The technology sense is not gradable — a thermostat is *smart* or it isn't.

senses.gloss: Intelligent, quick to understand.
examples: She's the *smartest* person in the room and she knows it.
That was a *smart* decision.

senses.gloss: Of a machine: controlled by a computer and able to react on its own.
examples: We put in a *smart* thermostat last winter.
The building runs on *smart* lighting that shuts itself off.

senses.gloss: Neat and stylish in appearance.
examples: He looked *smart* in a navy blazer.
The restaurant asks for *smart* casual dress.
